props.title: The Devil and Daniel Johnston
props.initialSlug: Portrait of outsider musician and artist

sections.content: **The Devil and Daniel Johnston** (2005) revolutionized music documentary storytelling by diving deep into mental illness and artistic genius. Director Jeff Feuerzeig crafts an intimate portrait using Johnston's extensive self-recorded audio diaries and Super 8 films, creating a raw authenticity that later influenced docs like **Amy** (2015) and **Kurt Cobain: Montage of Heck** (2015). The film shows Johnston's descent into severe bipolar disorder while creating hauntingly beautiful lo-fi music that influenced artists from Nirvana to The Flaming Lips.

sections.content: The film's innovative use of Johnston's personal archives created a template for modern music documentaries. **Kurt Cobain: Montage of Heck** (2015) followed suit with Cobain's journals and recordings, while **Amy** (2015) utilized intimate home videos. This approach of letting artists tell their own stories through archived materials has become standard practice, seen in recent docs like **Moonage Daydream** (2022) and **The Velvet Underground** (2021).

Mental health in music documentaries gained new depth after Johnston's story. **Brian Wilson: Long Promised Road** (2021) explores The Beach Boys genius's similar struggles with schizoaffective disorder, while **Whitney** (2018) examines Houston's battles with addiction and trauma. These films owe a debt to Feuerzeig's compassionate but unflinching approach to artist mental health. SUBHEAD: The Impact on Contemporary Music Documentaries

sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond subject matter to visual style. Johnston's crude animations and artwork inspired later docs to incorporate artist-created visuals, like **Brett Morgen's Cobain: Montage of Heck** (2015) and **Jane** (2017). This integration of personal artistic expression into documentary storytelling has become increasingly common, seen in works like **Billie Eilish: The World's A Little Blurry** (2021).
